label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
page_one_why: The numbers (814 commits, nine agents, one day) are striking and concrete, but page one says nothing about what it cost or what a business like mine gets out of it, and 'commit' and 'repository' needed the box to make sense.
what_the_team_did: Nine AI agents and one person built a whole talk, its slides, player and website in a single day, with every step recorded and a one-file brake that could stop them all.
why_it_matters_to_me: The stop-it-with-one-file idea and the plain-words rules page are things I could copy for my own staff-free admin work, but the pages never show a business task or a cost.
tomorrow: Write the one page of rules for one agent (what it is for, what it may touch, when it stops) for a back-office job like answering routine customer emails as drafts only, with me approving every send.

won_over.quote: Anyone on the team could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: That is a brake I understand in one breath, and it answers my fear of something running loose near customers.

won_over.quote: Write the one page of rules for your first agent tonight.
won_over.why: A small, concrete first step I could do this evening without buying or installing anything.

won_over.quote: You do not need to trust what I tell you about the day. You can open the day.
won_over.why: Checkable claims make me trust the author more than a sales pitch would.

stuck.quote: At 00:16 on 29 October 2026 I created an empty repository (C001).
stuck.why: The C001 style references in the middle of sentences break my reading; I do not know what they are until much later, and 'repository' is jargon on the very first line.

stuck.quote: Generation ZX is not a range of birth years.
stuck.why: The series branding paragraph delays the point and reads like marketing; I wanted the business benefit.

stuck.quote: Five steps. 1. An account and an empty repository.
stuck.why: I do not know where to make an account, which tool runs the agent, or what any of it costs per month.

stuck.quote: the hold gives my usage limit, at 95%, as the reason
stuck.why: Usage limit is the only sign of cost, and it is buried in a footnote with no pounds or dollars.

would_share: My operations manager, to ask whether the rules-page and brake idea could work for our order emails; not my accountant or customers, as there is no cost or customer-safety detail yet.

your_questions.a: Partly. The scale and speed hooked me, but there was no sign of what it cost or what it does for a business like mine.

your_questions.q: What would you hand to an agent tomorrow?
your_questions.a: Drafting replies to routine customer enquiries and tidying the weekly order summary, drafts only, nothing sent without me.

your_questions.q: What would stop you trusting it with a customer?
your_questions.a: No explanation of how an agent is kept from emailing or changing a customer's record by itself, and no mention of mistakes costing real money; the warning about public repositories and secrets helped, but the brake is shown only for the team, not for customer-facing work.

page_one.why: Strong numbers and a stage, but jargon and no cost or business payoff on the first page.

clarity.why: Short sections, boxes for the words, a clear five-step ending; claim ids interrupt the flow.

for_someone_like_me.why: It is about building a talk, not running a business with customers; I had to translate it myself.

would_start.why: The one-page rules exercise is easy to try, but without cost and customer-safety detail I would only try it on something internal.

notes: No text in the sample tried to direct me. The 'Where this came from' lines were read past as footers. I would want one sentence on monthly cost and one before-and-after of a small business task.
